text: Welcome to AI and Generative AI Fundamentals for Data Scientists. You already build models in Python. This course takes you from those models to the ones behind modern AI: neural networks, transformers, large language models, embeddings, and retrieval-augmented generation. It's working knowledge, not research. The AI Engineer path goes deeper if you want to build AI products.

We start with good news. A neural network isn't new magic. It's the regression you already know, repeated and stacked. A neuron takes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, then passes it through an activation function. Logistic regression is exactly that, with a sigmoid activation. It is a network with one neuron.

Here it is in numpy. Two features, two weights, and a bias. The dot product plus the bias gives zero point five. The sigmoid squeezes that into zero point six two. The weights here are invented for illustration; in a real model they're learned from data, which is what lesson three covers.

So what does stacking buy you? Take a ring-shaped dataset, where one group sits inside another. Fit a logistic regression, then a network with one hidden layer of eight neurons. Same data, same split, just a different model.

The results are stark. On held-out data the logistic regression scored zero point five four, barely better than a coin flip, because it can only draw one straight line. The eight-neuron network scored zero point nine nine, because its hidden layer bends the boundary around the inner group.

Here's the idea to keep. Each hidden neuron is its own small regression. The next layer treats their outputs as its features. So the network learns useful new features by itself, a bit like feature engineering the model does for you. More neurons means more capacity to bend.
That's the foundation. Next lesson we open up the parts of a network in detail: layers, activation functions, and loss.
